implements.nav: five entries — Summary, Decide, Understand, Bid, Submit — with the sections above as TABS inside them. DECIDE PRECEDES UNDERSTAND: "should we bid at all" outranks "can we deliver it", and the bid decision gates every other question. Build is labelled Bid — the thing being built on a pursuit is the RESPONSE, and "Build" was read as the delivery work, which is Understand's Delivery scope two entries away; the entry id stays `build` so shared links keep landing. Entry labels name intents and must never carry state: no active entry, no progress, no checkmarks, no numbering, and nothing in the pack may drive how an entry looks. Entry ids resolve as routes (#/b/<id>/decide) to whichever tab that reader last had open.
implements.persistentHeader: point person plus contributor chips carrying open-item counts (click filters Our readiness to that person), and ONE date rail: a horizontally scrollable sequence of every date the pack holds, in date order, each item carrying its own dot, name, date and days-from-now, with a dotted connector where two items fall on the same day. TODAY is an item in the sequence at its true place in the order; the strip opens scrolled so it sits one item in from the left, and arrows appear only when something is off-screen. The x-axis is ORDINAL, not linear time — no pixels-per-day both fits a 19-month programme on a screen and gives a one-week cluster room to write a name in — so intervals are STATED rather than drawn. There is no key list underneath: a name that is not on a dot was the defect this replaced. Nothing on it is hand-maintained, so nothing on it can rot.
implements.crossLinks: R-### on questions and Q-### on requirements, both ends; a jump opens whatever is collapsed, closed or filtered between the section and the row

changelog: 3.7.0 — THE CLIENT ZONE IS NAMED, AND EXECUTION FIT BECOMES A MEASUREMENT. "The client" is what the section is about to the TOOL; the reader wants the company, so the zone head is now "About <client>" and "Who we're talking to" is "Our contacts". OUR READ: "What this demands" and "What it's really about" were reported as reading like the same sentence twice, and the labels are why — both invite a summary of the opportunity, so /RFP obligingly wrote one into each. They are relabelled to name the two genuinely different questions, "What they want from us" (the artefact we would hand over) and "What winning turns on" (the thing that decides it), each with a helper line under the label, because a label alone was not enough to keep them apart. The pack fields are UNTOUCHED, so nothing already written is lost — this is a naming fix, not a schema change; if the two should genuinely become one field that is a /RFP decision, not a renderer one. EXECUTION FIT leaves the prose list: sitting as a third paragraph between two others it read as one more opinion, so it now gets a score out of 100 with its inputs drawn as bars, each input's basis stated beside it, the arithmetic printed underneath, and each bar linking to the tab its input came from — the same instrument as Response readiness, so nobody has to learn a second one. Both inputs are DERIVED from what the pack already holds and neither is defaulted: capability match is the share of the competency mix's weight that canonicalComp() can place onto our ten areas of expertise (the unplaced weight is work we would be reaching for, which on the first real pursuit correctly surfaced an AEM Sites gap), and signals is green over green-plus-red, with soft signals excluded on purpose so "we don't know" cannot move the number. A pack supporting one input says the score is a flag rather than a verdict; a pack supporting neither gets no score and says what it would need. The human's executionFit sentence stays, underneath the measurement it interprets.

3.6.3 — THE INTERVAL CHIPS COME OFF THE RAIL. Every item already prints its own date and its own days-from-now, so a "+5w" on each connector was ten numbers restating arithmetic the reader can do — "i can count on my own" — and each chip sat on the line where it had to be nudged clear of a dot to stop occluding it. The one relationship an evenly spaced ordinal axis genuinely CANNOT express is two items falling on the SAME day: spaced evenly they look exactly as far apart as two dates a year apart. So that case alone is drawn, and drawn rather than written — the earlier item of the pair renders its connector as a dotted line. The flag sits on the earlier one because each item draws the segment running to its right.

3.6.2 — THE MARGIN RESET WAS BEATING EVERY COMPONENT THAT IS A HEADING, PARAGRAPH OR LIST. `.rb h1, .rb h2, .rb h3, .rb h4, .rb p, .rb ul, .rb ol, .rb dl, .rb figure { margin: 0 }` scores one class plus one element, which outranks every single-class rule in this file — so `.rb-subhead { margin-top: 36px }` and `.rb-blockers { margin: 24px 0 36px }` have both computed to ZERO since the stylesheet was written, and nobody noticed because the failure is silent: the rule is there, it reads correctly, and it does nothing. That is why the readiness blockers sat flush against the cards above them and "What we need from you" sat flush against the blockers, and why tightening the tiles in 3.6.1 did not fix what was actually reported. The reset is now wrapped in :where(), which scores zero, so it ties with a component rule and loses on source order — the behaviour every rule below it was written expecting. This restores intended margins across the whole renderer, not just this tab; every section was walked at 1500 and 1180 to confirm nothing that had been relying on the reset blew out. Also: `.rb-subhead:first-of-type { margin-top: 0 }` correctly suppresses the margin on a subhead that OPENS a section, and wrongly suppressed it on Our readiness, where the first h3 follows the pulse row and the blockers — `.rb-blockers + .rb-subhead` and `.rb-zone + .rb-subhead` give it back.

3.6.1 — PULSE TILE SPACING. The two tiles stretched to a shared height and `.rb-expand { margin-top: auto }` then pinned the shorter one's disclosure to the bottom of that borrowed height — so opening "How this is computed" on Response readiness left Critical path a mostly empty box with its own summary stranded 200px below its last line. Stretch is right while both are closed (two tiles of one height read as a pair, and the shorter simply carries a little space under its last line) and wrong the moment either opens, so `:has(.rb-expand[open])` switches the row to align-items:start; a browser without :has() keeps the stretch, which is the behaviour it has today. Inside a tile the disclosure now hugs its own content — auto margin turned whatever slack was left into a gap between the bar and the summary whose size depended on what was in the OTHER card, so the rhythm changed as you read. The breakdown rows drop from the shared 9px row padding to 6px: they are small facts, not a data table, and four of them at requirement height turned a two-line explanation into a scroll. Tile padding evened to 16/18/14, and the pulse row gets --rb-s3 of air under the section heading instead of the inline margin-top:0 it was carrying.

3.6.0 — THE DATE RAIL BECOMES AN ORDINAL SEQUENCE, AND EVERY NAME SITS ON ITS OWN DOT. Three designs failed on the same rock. Names ON a linear axis were truncated at every width, because real dates cluster: three inside one week and one nineteen months out. Moving them to a key underneath (3.4.2) made them legible and cut the tie to the dots — on a real pursuit that was eleven rows wrapping into three ragged columns, with no way to tell which row was which dot, which is exactly how it was reported: "these timeline bullets are super messy... only offer text if it's associated to a dot on the timeline". Scrolling the axis at a fixed pixels-per-day (3.5.0) fixed the far dates and did nothing for the cluster: at 7px a day, three dates in one week sit 21px apart and their labels still cannot coexist. There is no pixels-per-day that both fits a 19-month programme on a screen and gives a one-week cluster room to write in. So the x-axis stops being linear time. Items sit in date order, evenly, each carrying its dot, name, date and days-from-now, and the interval to the previous item is PRINTED on the connector — "+12mo" cannot be misread the way a long empty stretch can, which is the same reason the two-clock split exists. TODAY is an item in the sequence at its true place in the order, so what has passed still reads at a glance; the strip opens scrolled so TODAY sits one item in, keeping the immediate past as context for what is next. Arrows scroll by 80% of the pane and hide themselves when everything fits (with two pixels of slack, because sub-pixel layout otherwise lights an arrow that does nothing). The key list is gone: one instrument, one ordering. The header is ~100px shorter on a pursuit carrying a client programme. Labels clamp at two lines — /RFP legitimately writes a full sentence into a date label, and unclamped it made one item four times the height of its neighbours; the whole string is on the item's title and in the Timeline tab. FIXED IN THE SAME PASS: the gap chip was centred on the item's left edge, which is exactly where that item's dot is — the chip is opaque, so every dot but the first vanished and the rail read as a line with no points on it. It now sits just before the dot it leads to. And the opening scroll position was computed from offsetLeft, which reports against the nearest positioned ancestor rather than the scroller, so it landed a couple of hundred pixels past the item it was aimed at; it is measured from rects now, over two animation frames rather than one, because the widths it depends on are not final until the frame after layout. scroll-snap was removed for the same reason — proximity snapping dragged the programmatic opening position to the nearest item boundary.

3.5.0 — COLLAPSED BY DEFAULT, DECIDE FIRST, AND A TIMELINE THAT SCROLLS. (1) Every group opens CLOSED and the stored set now records what a person has OPENED rather than what they closed. Expanded-by-default meant Our readiness opened as eight owner groups of rows, Effort & team as four full tables and Delivery scope as every theme at once; a tab that opens as a wall gets scrolled, not read. Closed, the same tab opens as its own contents page — every heading with its count. The storage key moved from rb.qcollapse to rb.gopen with the meaning: reusing it would have read every previously-closed group as a request to OPEN it, and an inverted preference is worse than none. Plain groups (Proposed team, Named so far, Competencies, Key personnel, Criteria for success, the Decision log's three) went through the same control via a new groupBlock(), so a section reads the same whether its blocks are filterable lists or plain tables. (2) NAV: Decide moves ahead of Understand and Build is labelled Bid. "Should we bid at all" gates every other question, and putting the evidence for that call after the work that only matters if it goes our way was the wrong priority order; Build named the delivery work rather than the response, which is what the entry actually holds. Entry ids are untouched. (3) THE RAIL PLOTS EVERY DATE AND SCROLLS. It plotted our response dates only, because on a fixed-width axis a pursuit running 19 months collapses everything happening this month into 4% of the width. Sized in pixels per day inside a scroll container, that trade disappears: a long program is a long track, near dates keep real distance, and the container opens scrolled so TODAY sits a quarter of the way in. The client's program is no longer a folded second list under the key — it is in the one key, in date order, drawn hollow, and now on the track too. (4) A JUMP LANDS: reveal() opens every collapsed group, closed disclosure and active filter between the section and the row it was sent to, then opens the row's own disclosure — scrollIntoView on a hidden element scrolls nowhere, which read as a broken link, and with everything collapsed that became the common case. (5) Q-### BACK-REFERENCES on requirements, numbered by the same orderedQuestions() the Questions tab numbers with, so the thread reads in both directions instead of one. FIXED: the roster's "Role on the bid" column. Its cells and its grid vars disagreed — the role value sat in a 0px column while its heading sat over the delete-button column — so every role broke one word per line down a 40px gutter. FIXED: .rb-pulse had display:grid only under .rb-snapshot, so Response readiness and Critical path were a two-column row on Summary and a pair of full-width cards jammed together on Our readiness. FIXED: Summary was capped at 48rem, which narrowed the one screen everybody reads to two thirds of the pane to solve a prose-measure problem; the cap is now on the ask prose, where it belongs.

3.4.3 — DAYS ARE COUNTED IN LOCAL CALENDAR DAYS. daysFromNow() was Math.ceil() over a raw millisecond difference, which returns -0 for a date that passed less than a day ago at any positive UTC offset — and `-0 < 0` is FALSE, which is the exact test every late/overdue check on this renderer makes: the late-item counts on the header chips and on Our readiness, the at-risk row status, the deadline pill and the date rail all agreed with each other and were all wrong for one day, for readers east of Greenwich. The second half of the same fault is quieter and hit everyone: a date-only pack value ("2026-01-30", which is what /RFP emits for every date except the submission) parses as UTC MIDNIGHT, so comparing it against local midnight was off by the reader's offset in either direction and a date could read one day early or late depending on who opened the brief. Date-only strings are now parsed as local dates, anything carrying a time is reduced to the local calendar day it falls on, and the subtraction is rounded rather than ceiled because a DST day is 23 or 25 hours long. A deadline at 5pm today now reads 0 days rather than 1 — which is what "Due today" already claimed. The hub carries the identical localDay() in app.js; the two must stay in step, because the Library card and the brief header state the same countdown.

3.4.2 — The header date strip splits into a TRACK and a KEY, and now lists every date the pack holds rather than only the plotted ones. Names used to sit on the time axis, and measured across 1100-1680px three of four were truncated at EVERY width while both end labels hung past the track — because real response dates cluster (three inside one week, one two months out) and a linear axis hands the most room to the stretch where nothing happens. 3.4.1's lane stacking stopped the collisions and could never make the labels legible; that was the symptom, this is the instrument. Dots keep their exact position, so a cluster still looks like a cluster; names moved to a wrapping key underneath with the date and days-from-now on every row, where nothing has to be truncated. ALL dates are listed, which is new — the client's six program dates are folded behind a native
rather than dropped. They are still not PLOTTED, and that is a scale decision rather than an editorial one: this pursuit runs from 6 days ago to 570 days out, so drawing a go-live 19 months away beside a submission in 13 days collapses the four dates that matter this month into 3.6% of the width — the exact failure the two-clock split exists to stop, where the far date reads as slack on the near one. TODAY is a marker again: its rule ran the full height of the strip and read as a panel divider splitting the header in two. CONTACTS: name on its own line, role beneath in helper text, laid out on a grid. They were inline-flex on a shared baseline, which staggered the moment a name wrapped — "Angela Galmarini" broke to two lines and the role started level with its SECOND line, so the group read as a staircase with no line clearly belonging to anyone. They stay s made block by CSS because the block sits inside a

, where a

    is hoisted out by the parser. And "reporting to" became a labelled "Reports to:" value: /RFP legitimately writes a sentence into reportsTo when the documents do not say, which rendered as "...reporting to Not stated in the documents." Fixing the grammar beats guessing which strings mean absent.

3.4.1 — Rail lane height was 22px, which clears a ONE-line label and not the two-line one the clamp allows (2 x 11px x 1.25 = 28px). Every test pack happened to carry short date labels; the first real pursuit had "Budgetary pricing and costed options to Angela" and it bled 6px into the lane below. Two dates falling on the same day is what forces stacking in the first place, so this is the common path and not an edge case. Lane step is now a token, --rb-lane-h: 30px, used by the label offset, the leader line and the track height together — they were three separate 22px literals and would have drifted apart on the next change.

3.4.0 — SCHEMA v5, and the nav stops being a list of everything. schemaSupport is now {min:1,max:5}; /RFP emits v5 and the 4->5 migration is a pure version bump, because everything v5 adds (competencyMix, pointPerson, industry, bidValue, outcome) is knowledge a v4 pack does not contain and inventing it would poison the portfolio charts it exists to feed. NAV: ten sections under four group headings read as overload, and the density sat in the wrong place — a sidebar is for choosing a job, not enumerating every view that job might need. Five entries now (Summary, Understand, Decide, Build, Submit) with the sections as tabs inside them. Summary is entry one rather than chrome floating above the groups, because ungrouped meant skipped; it is no longer called TLDR, which told a first-time reader nothing. Understand moves ahead of Decide now the triage read happens on Summary itself. Every section id and alias survives; routes resolve pane -> entry -> tab and the active tab persists per pursuit per person. `rules` is NOT an alias and must never become one. PERSISTENT HEADER: the people and a derived response-date rail with a TODAY marker, true on every tab. The rail's span always includes today — scaling it to the dates alone looked right and was useless in the commonest case there is, a live pursuit where every date is still ahead of you and the marker never drew. Dots hold their exact position and labels step down a lane when they would collide, because nudging the dots would fix the picture by making the rail lie about the one thing it claims to show. COMPETENCY MIX leads Summary, and "Who's involved" is gone (its people moved to the header): a competency leader opens a brief to learn whether the bid needs them and how much — "I see that I'm representing 5% of the bid, I'm going to back off." One hue at descending tints, never a categorical palette; a donut only where a donut is honest (<=5 slices, none under 5%); every weight editable, which flips competencyMix.source to human. Absent from the pack it is derived from team.competencies hours, and failing that from the dead `fte` field — not a resurrection of FTE as a displayed number, which is what was killed, but its ratios, so the flagship section is not empty on the entire pre-v5 library. The basis is always stated on screen. FIXED: the "Mine" filter showed every OWNED row to everybody. `[data-filter=mine][data-mine] li[data-owner]` matches any row that has an owner — CSS cannot compare one attribute's value to another's — and it failed silently: the chip lit, rows vanished, and what remained looked plausible. Rows are now stamped data-mine at render time, so filtering stays a pure CSS state flip.

3.3.1 — TLDR drops "What's needed next". It listed the five nearest open action items with owner and due date — which is the top of the Our readiness checklist, rendered a second time in a bespoke row shape, on the one tab that is supposed to be a read-out rather than a work surface. The reader who needs those rows is the person who owns one, and the strip at the top of TLDR already carries them straight to their rows in Our readiness. Nothing is lost; one place to keep true is gained. The `.rb-needs` component and its derived `blockers`/`openCount`/`unowned` values are gone with it.

3.3.0 — THE CLIENT, on TLDR. Three things the brief never said and a reader needed: what the company actually does, which team inside it we are in contact with (function plus named contacts, each add/edit/deletable), and the business problem behind the RFP. Without them the ask lands with no ground under it — you could read the whole tab and still not know what business you would be serving. Reads from a new `clientContext` block: {business, team:{name,reportsTo}, contacts:[{name,role}], problem}. Placed between the ask prose and Our read, using the same label/value grid as the verdict so there is no new component to learn. The overlap with 'what it's really about' is resolved by ALTITUDE, not by deleting one: that line stays on Our read as our one-sentence strategic angle, while `clientContext.problem` carries the client's business problem in full — what is broken today, what it costs them, why now. The test is that either should still make sense to a reader who skipped the other.

3.2.1 — the TLDR reads as one column. The ask paragraphs were capped at the 66ch prose measure while the deadline rule, the verdict table and the zone headings ran the full 72rem column, so the prose stopped about 60% of the way across with everything above and below it running wider. That reads as a broken layout rather than a considered measure, and it was the first thing reported on a real pursuit. One max-width on .rb-snapshot instead: 48rem keeps the ask at roughly 75 characters a line — the measure the 66ch cap was protecting — and every block on the tab now shares a right edge. Lists and tables elsewhere still run to 72rem, because they are data, not prose.

Group order is Decide → Understand → Build → Submit: "should we bid" outranks "can we build it", because the bid decision gates every other question. Reading order is PRIORITY, not chronology — the labels are intents, so nothing implies you passed through one group to reach the next. 3.2.0 — Effort & team becomes a PROPOSED TEAM. It was a list of competency hours and a reader could not tell what it was for ("I do want a little bit more clarity on what this does"); hours are an abstraction, a team is what a bid actually proposes. Each row is a role: level (Junior/Mid/Senior), geography (US onshore / Nearshore LATAM / Offshore India / EMEA), remote or on-site, heads, analog and AI-assisted hours, and pay and bill rates that those four attributes imply — with margin derived per row and in total, and the existing analog/AI toggle now driving cost and revenue as well as hours. /RFP proposes the team sized LEAN and estimates rates from role x level x geography x mode, stating the basis under each row so a human can argue with it; everything is editable. The competency table stays underneath as the mapping layer, with the purpose finally stated on screen — it routes requirement IDs to the right lead so the wrong people are not in the meeting. The "outside our ten areas of expertise" flag is GONE: it was read as "we can't do that", a capability denial, when it only ever meant the name did not match our taxonomy. Column headers added wherever a table was a grid of values with nothing naming the columns — the requirement-ID column beside each competency being the one that got reported. Pre-flight is renamed Submission check and Record is renamed Decision log: in cold-reading the nav a participant named eight of ten sections unprompted and said of those two, "I'm not too sure of". Section ids are unchanged.

3.0.0 — IA v3. The eight flat tabs now sort by ONE axis, the job you came to do, under four group headings: Understand / Decide / Build / Submit. TLDR stays ungrouped above them and Documents stays chrome below them. THE GROUP LABELS NAME INTENTS, NEVER STATES — no active group, no progress, no numbering, and nothing in the pack may drive their appearance, because a lifecycle in a nav is how the old six-step stage stepper became a lie. Rules & Requirements splits back into two tabs, since the split IS the difference: `rules` (Rules of the bid, governs the bid, read-only) and `compliance` (Delivery scope, what we deliver if we win). `compliance` keeps its id because shared links pointed at requirements, and `rules` stops being a SECTION_ALIAS so old #/…/rules links land on the right half. Program dates move from readiness to Delivery scope, so each view carries ONE clock: the kind filter chips and the two-color key are gone as redundant, and the TODAY marker no longer appears on the client's own dates. NEW: Pre-flight, the view for the moment of submitting — deadline, format and delivery, a one-time confirmation pass over the rules (writing `rules[].checked`, the field nothing had read since the rules checklist was removed, because a pass genuinely completes where a rule never does), anything still open, and the attachment list. TLDR gains one strip naming what is waiting on you, shown only when we know who is reading and they own something open. The host now lands you on the section you last visited per pursuit; first-time readers still get TLDR. Renames: Readiness→Our readiness, Scorecard→Scoring & fit, Team & Burden→Effort & team, Questions→Questions to client, and every page title now matches its nav item. Rules of the bid and Delivery scope are now formatted as siblings: both group their rows through listBlock and both put date content in a fold rendered by the same timeline() component. Rules group by `rules[].category` (Eligibility / Format & limits / Required forms / Delivery), inferred from the label when absent, with anything unplaceable in a visible Unclassified group — the rules collection had been attracting strategy notes and evaluation criteria, and a flat list hid them. Design-system pass so no section needs re-learning: risks and signals now go through listBlock like every other list (listBlock gained a second filter axis, `axis:"sev"`, giving risks High/Medium/Low chips with the same CSS-flip behavior as status), the bespoke signal list with colored dashes for bullets is gone — direction is carried by the group name, which is unambiguous — severity moved into the shared row's id column, and the risk detail's two prose blocks are labeled "Proposed mitigation" and "How we answer it in the proposal" instead of sitting unlabeled. ONE disclosure chevron for the whole brief: the expander drew a CSS chevron while folds and collapse headers rendered a solid triangle from a .rb-caret span, and the risk summary carried both at once — that was the double caret, not a native browser marker. .rb-caret survives only on the export menu, which is not a disclosure. Competencies map legacy free-text names onto the ten areas of expertise ON READ (Cyber → DevSecOps & Service Management, QA → Quality & Test Automation, and so on), leading with the canonical area and keeping the pack's original wording underneath as "stated as …", so pursuits imported before the vocabulary closed read correctly without a re-run; a name that cannot be placed with confidence stays unmapped rather than guessed at. EVERYTHING IS EDITABLE: roster, competencies, key personnel, requirements, scoring criteria, success criteria, signals, decisions, parking lot and meetings all gained add/edit/delete. That needed three changes underneath — applyOverrides removes by any field (`itemKey`, or `@index` for arrays of plain strings), setByPath accepts positional selectors and nested collection paths, and add/remove resolve dotted collections like `team.competencies` instead of writing to a literal key nothing reads. Pre-flight stays read-only apart from its rule ticks, because everything on it is derived from other sections.

2.2.0 — naming and modelling pass, all of it correction rather than rename. Plan becomes READINESS and argues from the number down: score, then the linked blockers that explain it (deriveReadiness().gaps now returns {text,goto,el} objects), then the checklist, then the dates last because dates are the frame not the content. Compliance becomes RULES & REQUIREMENTS and the split is stated: 'To bid at all, we must obey this' / 'If we win, we deliver this' — miss a rule and the bid is discarded unread, miss a requirement and you priced work you cannot do. A RULE IS NOT A TASK: the rules checkbox, the 'N of M confirmed' count and the readiness input built on `checked` are gone, so readiness has two honest inputs instead of three with one invented. The must/mandatory/gate chips are gone everywhere; `mandatory` stays in the data because rowStatus() derives atRisk from it. The coverage matrix is gone. Scorecard becomes EVALUATION SCORECARD. FTE is gone from Team & Burden, replaced by two hour estimates per competency — hours (analog) and hoursAi — with a chip toggle and the saving as a percentage, offered only when the pack carries hoursAi. Competencies are a closed vocabulary: the ten Experis areas of expertise in published order, off-menu entries rendered and flagged. Two CSS faults fixed that had silently disabled every filter chip's border: a class selector losing to the `.rb button {border:0}` reset, and the never-defined --rb-rule token.

2.1.0 — three fixes and one behavior change. (1) KEY DATES carry a kind: response dates are ours to hit, program dates are the client's own, and the two are color-coded with a key and filtered one at a time — a rail mixing 'in 4 days' with 'in 14 months' made the far date read as slack on the near one. dates[].kind is honoured where the pack states it and inferred from the label where it does not; the countdown tile's 'Next' now ignores program dates, which is why it was pointing at a milestone a year out. (2) TICK TO CLOSE: action items, requirements and submission rules can be marked done from read mode. Closing a row was behind the edit button, which is a mode you have to know exists; the tick writes the same override and the same activity row. (3) The Plan tab's 'who's carrying what' heatmap is gone — on a real pursuit it was a grid of ones and zeroes above a checklist already grouped by owner. Also: data-goto anchors now carry their real route instead of href='#', one heading over Key dates instead of two, and a document link the site is carrying resolves on click rather than blocking first paint on every attached PDF.

2.0.0 — the V2 information architecture, from four user-feedback sessions. Twelve nav sections become EIGHT: Snapshot absorbs The Ask (Scope); Key Dates + Action Checklist become Plan; Rules & Constraints + Requirements become Compliance; Evaluation + Pass/Fail Gates become Scorecard; Decisions & Parking Lot becomes Record, last. Document Map leaves the nav and sits as a separate launcher at its foot. Every list now shares one component: filter chips driven by its own statuses plus Mine, collapsible groups with persisted state, and a three-state status token (done | open | atRisk) that means the same thing everywhere — filtering is a CSS state flip, never a re-render, so it cannot disturb edit mode or fight live sync. Team & Burden estimates in HOURS not fractional FTE, with effort distribution; 'Current load' renamed because it read as personal availability. Risk detail collapses behind an expander and renders a suggested strategic response. Soft signals replaces 'beige'. The 'must' chip is suppressed when every row carries it. Old section routes (ask, checklist, dates, rules, requirements) resolve through aliases so shared links survive.

1.2.0 — live edit sync: elements, activity and the pursuit index now stream over onSnapshot instead of being read once at load, so another person's edit reaches the open brief without a reload. Remote changes park while a field is focused and land on blur, so a re-render can never eat what someone is typing. Comment listener reconnects with backoff instead of degrading permanently on one blip. schemaSupport raised to 4. editMode declared honestly — it shipped in 1.1.x but the manifest still said false.
1.1.0 — visual craft pass: one type scale, one row grid, one chip system, controlled measure, masthead + countdown pill, inline source disclosure, AA-safe greys.
1.0.0 — first release: 12 sections read mode, four derived components, document previews.
notes: Fetch renderer.js + renderer.css from this directory and inline both to build a standalone brief. Do not fork — improvements here re-render every hosted pursuit on redeploy. Section IDS are preserved across the 12->8 merge and SECTION_ALIASES maps the retired ones, because #/b/<pursuit>/requirements links are already shared in Teams threads; a tidier id set is not worth a dead link. Document bytes are base64-chunked into pursuits/{briefId}/files — deploy firestore.rules alongside a renderer that expects them, or every fetch fails closed. Relationships to the buying/grading panel is the one feature gap named in testing and is deliberately NOT built: hand-typed relationship data is stale by the second pursuit. It lands as its own tab under Decide when there is a CRM to read it from.
